Aneutronic fusion builds off of the z-pinch experiments of the early 2000's. No giant steam turbine required, allowing for reactors to be built at large and small scales, making it suitable for powering marine vessels, aircraft, spacecraft, data centers and industrial hubs.

Two US companies. Trump Media & Technology Group bought TAE Technologies recently. Trump's sons have insider information, they know what's coming. Then there is American Fusion (AMFN) (formerly Kepler Fusion) which was recently spun off out of the US Navy ONR.

AMFN is publicly traded on the OTC, it recycled an existing shell corp and ISIN, so ignore the stock's price chart prior to June 2025. The technology is being made available from the ONR via a public company specifically to remove conflicts of interest. This is the only publicly traded fusion company. On Friday afternoon, they announced they have just completed initial phase of 3rd party validation and testing at Texas Tech University w/ Fermilab oversight, achieving successful fusion reaction and plasma generation. Zero radiation emissions detected.

Sustained pulsed plasma generation to power electrical induction is next. Maybe it fails, maybe it succeeds.

I bought myself a lottery ticket.

The “Panda Daytona” is the white-dial Rolex Daytona chronograph (black subdials on a white face, resembling a panda).

* Secondary market: often $30k–40k+, sometimes more depending on the reference and market.

That huge gap means receiving one from an AD is like being handed an asset that’s immediately worth tens of thousands more than you paid.

Why did this person buy all those other watches?

They’ve purchased approximately:

* 4 Rolexes
* 2 Cartiers
* 1 Breitling
* 1 Tudor

…plus another 3–4 watches for friends and family.

This is called building purchase history.

The idea is:

“I’ve spent well over $100,000 with your store. When the rare Daytona arrives, remember me.”

Many luxury dealers reward repeat customers before first-time buyers.

Why is the AD saying “you’re not there yet”?

The dealer is essentially saying:

“You’re a good customer, but not one of our very best customers.”

From the dealer’s perspective, they may have clients who have spent:

* $250,000
* $500,000
* $1 million+

Those customers often receive the rarest allocations first.

Why not just sell it to whoever asks first?

Because Rolex supplies far fewer Daytonas than demand.

If a dealer receives only 5–20 Panda Daytonas per year but has hundreds of interested customers, someone has to choose who gets them
